title: Ace: GitHub Next's open-source tool for multiplayer agentic development
content:
Agents run as you, with a shell on your Mac. Read this first.
Your tailnet is the team. Everyone on it who runs Ace is on your team. Teammates see each other’s channels in the projects they can access, and join them.
Bring your own Anthropic or OpenAI key. It stays in your keychain.
Join a teammate’s work and drive their agents; they join yours and drive yours. Everyone sees the same conversation as it happens.
Agents work where your work already is, with everything your Mac has. Build a native app and watch it run beside the chat. There’s no VM to set up and nothing to keep in sync.
gh. Each piece of work gets its own lane of your repo.
A channel runs on one host. Channel traffic goes from host to host over your tailnet. The directory, a small service your team deploys, only answers “who has which channel”, so a channel stays listed when its host is asleep, and the app shows it as offline instead of losing it. Optionally, a cloud channel lives in your team’s own account and keeps working with every lid closed; see get started.
Ace doesn’t run any servers for you. Your team deploys one small service, the directory, to its own account, so everyone shares one view of the team’s channels whether or not any one Mac is awake.‡
Local access means a shell on your machine. Channels and lanes are not sandboxes.
Ace runs agents with the privileges of the user running the host. They can execute shell commands and change files beyond the project. Turning on a channel’s agent access lets teammates run commands on its host; it starts off.
Only work this way with people you’d trust with the machine. Work together over Tailscale, and keep the host’s gateway on loopback or your private tailnet. Never expose it to the public internet.
Ace is an experiment from GitHub Next in real-time, multiplayer agentic development. It started in the cloud; this version runs on your own machine, so anyone can run it and invite their team. It’s built in Ace: every change is made in a channel, on a lane, and lands as a pull request.
It’s MIT licensed and there’s no service behind it. Clone it, change what doesn’t suit your team, add the hosting provider you need. Expect rough edges; it moves fast, and we’d love to hear what you find.
‡ A deployed directory runs on Cloudflare Workers, Fly.io, or celld on machines your team runs. Cloud channels need Cloudflare Workers and Containers for now. Other providers may follow, and you can add one by forking Ace or sending a pull request.

report.summary: GitHub Next releases Ace, an open-source tool for real-time multiplayer agentic development, enabling teams to share AI agent sessions with local shell access over Tailscale.
report.background: The integration of AI agents into software development is evolving from single-user assistants to collaborative team tools. GitHub Next, GitHub's research arm, explores future workflows. Ace addresses the gap in real-time collaboration on agentic tasks, where multiple developers can share context and control. Unlike cloud-based solutions, Ace runs agents locally on each developer's machine, leveraging existing environments and API keys. It uses Tailscale for secure peer-to-peer networking, avoiding central servers. This aligns with trends of local-first development and privacy-conscious AI. Ace is an experiment, MIT licensed, and built using itself, reflecting GitHub Next's iterative approach. It aims to make agentic development a shared, interactive experience, similar to pair programming but with AI agents.
key_points: Ace enables real-time multiplayer collaboration: team members on the same Tailscale network can join each other's channels, drive agents, and see the same conversation live. Each piece of work gets its own lane in the repo, and channels are hosted on a teammate's machine, with a small directory service tracking ownership.

Agents run locally with full shell access: each agent operates with the user's privileges on their Mac, using their own Anthropic or OpenAI API key stored in the keychain. There's no VM; agents work directly in the local environment, building native apps and watching them run beside the chat.

Security is user-managed: since agents have shell access, users must trust their teammates. Agent access for teammates starts off and should only be enabled with trusted individuals. Hosts should keep gateways on loopback or private tailnet, never exposed publicly. This emphasizes careful team trust management.

Ace is open-source and extensible: MIT licensed with no central service, teams deploy a small directory service to their own account (e.g., Cloudflare Workers, Fly.io, celld). Built using Ace itself, every change lands as a pull request. Teams can fork and modify it, adding hosting providers as needed.
report.impact: Ace signals a shift towards collaborative, local-first AI agent workflows, potentially boosting team productivity by enabling shared context and real-time intervention. For developers, it offers a customizable, open-source alternative to proprietary cloud-based agent platforms, though security concerns require careful trust management. Regular users may see more interactive AI coding tools emerge, but the shell access requirement limits Ace to technical teams. The emphasis on local execution and peer-to-peer networking could influence future AI tools to prioritize data privacy and user control, challenging the dominance of centralized cloud services in AI-assisted development.
report.tools: Ace itself is the primary tool; follow GitHub Next for updates. For secure networking, Tailscale is essential. Cloudflare Workers and Containers are needed for cloud channels; Fly.io and celld are alternatives for the directory. For similar collaborative coding, VS Code Live Share offers real-time sharing but lacks agentic features. Open-source agentic projects like OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) and Continue.dev provide AI coding assistance but not multiplayer. Ace's MIT license encourages experimentation, so watch for community forks and extensions.
